pos: adj. (made of clay; rendering Hebrew cheres, Greek ostrakinos)
etymology: From earth. An earthen vessel is fired clay — cheap, common, breakable, and in Paul's hands the whole doctrine of ministry.
biblical_def: Earthen means made of clay. Paul states the arrangement: “we have this treasure in earthen vessels, that the excellency of the power may be of God, and not of us” (2Co 4:7). Jeremiah is told to buy the evidence of a field and put the deeds “in an earthen vessel, that they may continue many days” (Jer 32:14). The law says an earthen vessel touched by uncleanness must be broken (Lev 11:33), and Jeremiah breaks a potter's earthen bottle as a sign (Jer 19:1,10).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines earthen as made of earth; made of clay; as an earthen vessel; earthen ware.
webster_full: EARTHEN, a. Made of earth; made of clay; as an earthen vessel; earthen ware.
scriptures: But we have this treasure in earthen vessels, that the excellency of the power may be of God, and not of us.

Thus saith the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel; Take these evidences, this evidence of the purchase, both which is sealed, and this evidence which is open; and put them in an earthen vessel, that they may continue many days.
And every earthen vessel, whereinto any of them falleth, whatsoever is in it shall be unclean; and ye shall break it.
Then shalt thou break the bottle in the sight of the men that go with thee,
corruption_summary: Ministry is judged by the impressiveness of the minister, and Paul says the container was chosen cheap on purpose so nobody would confuse it with the contents.
corruption_paragraphs: 2 Corinthians 4:7 gives the reason for the mismatch: but we have this treasure in earthen vessels, that the excellency of the power may be of God, and not of us. The pairing is deliberate. A treasure in a gold box invites admiration of the box; the same treasure in a clay pot leaves no ambiguity about where the value lies. Paul then lists what happens to the pot — troubled on every side, perplexed, persecuted, cast down — and insists none of it destroys the contents.

Jeremiah 32:14 uses an earthen vessel for the opposite property: put them in an earthen vessel, that they may continue many days. Clay is fragile in the hand and remarkably durable in the ground; the deeds to a field in a doomed country were stored in the cheapest available container precisely because it would outlast the exile. Fragility and endurance in the same material is a fair description of the church.
roots_summary: Hebrew cheres (H2789), earthenware, a potsherd; Greek ostrakinos (G3749), made of clay — from ostrakon, a shard.
roots_lines: Greek ostrakinos (G3749) — earthen; 2 Corinthians 4:7, 2 Timothy 2:20.
Hebrew cheres (H2789) — earthenware, potsherd; Leviticus 11:33, Jeremiah 19:1.
Greek huperbole (G5236) — excellency, surpassing greatness; 2 Corinthians 4:7.
usage: “This treasure in earthen vessels” — the container chosen cheap on purpose.
“That the excellency of the power may be of God, and not of us” — the stated reason.
“Put them in an earthen vessel, that they may continue many days” — fragile and durable at once.

pos: adj. (belonging to this world; rendering Greek epigeios)
etymology: From earth. Earthly in the New Testament is not a synonym for physical but for what is bounded by this world's horizon.
biblical_def: Earthly means belonging to this world. Christ tells Nicodemus, “If I have told you earthly things, and ye believe not, how shall ye believe, if I tell you of heavenly things?” (Joh 3:12). Paul contrasts two houses: “if our earthly house of this tabernacle were dissolved, we have a building of God” (2Co 5:1). He warns of those “who mind earthly things” (Php 3:19), and James says a certain wisdom is “earthly, sensual, devilish” (Jas 3:15).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines earthly as pertaining to the earth, or to this world; not heavenly or spiritual; belonging to our present state; and vile, mean, sordid.
webster_full: EARTHLY, a. Pertaining to the earth, or to this world.
2. Not heavenly; vile; mean; as this earthly load of clay.
3. Belonging to our present state; as earthly objects; earthly residence.
4. Corporeal; not mental.
scriptures: Joh 3:12
If I have told you earthly things, and ye believe not, how shall ye believe, if I tell you of heavenly things?
For we know that if our earthly house of this tabernacle were dissolved, we have a building of God, an house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens.
Php 3:19
Whose end is destruction, whose God is their belly, and whose glory is in their shame, who mind earthly things.)
Jas 3:15
This wisdom descendeth not from above, but is earthly, sensual, devilish.
corruption_summary: Earthly is read as a synonym for material and therefore suspect, and James applies it to a wisdom — something entirely mental that is still bounded by this world.
corruption_paragraphs: James 3:15 puts earthly first in a descending sequence: this wisdom descendeth not from above, but is earthly, sensual, devilish. The thing being described is wisdom — advice, strategy, insight. It is not condemned for being practical but for having no horizon beyond this world, and James says where envying and strife is, there is confusion and every evil work. The test he offers is what the wisdom produces in a room.

John 3:12 shows Christ using earthly as a starting point rather than an insult: if I have told you earthly things, and ye believe not, how shall ye believe, if I tell you of heavenly things? He had been speaking of birth — something Nicodemus could observe. Unbelief at the observable level is not remedied by escalating to the invisible, which is worth remembering by anyone tempted to answer scepticism with mystery.
roots_summary: Greek epigeios (G1919), upon the earth, earthly; choikos (G5517), of dust — the earthy man of 1 Corinthians 15:47.
roots_lines: Greek epigeios (G1919) — earthly; John 3:12, 2 Corinthians 5:1, Philippians 3:19, James 3:15.
Greek choikos (G5517) — earthy, of dust; 1 Corinthians 15:47-49.
Greek epouranios (G2032) — heavenly; the contrasting term in each passage.
usage: “If I have told you earthly things, and ye believe not” — unbelief at the observable level.
“Our earthly house of this tabernacle” — a tent, against a building of God.
“Earthly, sensual, devilish” — a wisdom with no horizon.

pos: adj. (skilled in speech; rendering Hebrew debarim, Greek logios)
etymology: From Latin eloqui, to speak out. Eloquence in Scripture is a real gift, an honest disqualification, and never the ground of power.
biblical_def: Eloquent means skilled in speech. Moses pleads its absence: “O my Lord, I am not eloquent… but I am slow of speech, and of a slow tongue” (Exo 4:10), and God answers, “Who hath made man's mouth?” (Exo 4:11). Apollos is introduced as “an eloquent man, and mighty in the scriptures” (Act 18:24) — and is still taken aside and taught more perfectly by a tentmaker and his wife (Act 18:26).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines eloquent as having the power of oratory; speaking with fluency, propriety, elegance and animation; and composed with elegance and spirit.
webster_full: ELOQUENT, a. Having the power of oratory; speaking with fluency, propriety, elegance and animation; as an eloquent orator.
2. Composed with elegance and spirit; elegant and animated; adapted to please, affect and persuade; as an eloquent address.
scriptures: Exo 4:10
And Moses said unto the LORD, O my Lord, I am not eloquent, neither heretofore, nor since thou hast spoken unto thy servant: but I am slow of speech, and of a slow tongue.
Exo 4:11
And the LORD said unto him, Who hath made man's mouth? or who maketh the dumb, or deaf, or the seeing, or the blind? have not I the LORD?
And a certain Jew named Apollos, born at Alexandria, an eloquent man, and mighty in the scriptures, came to Ephesus.
And he began to speak boldly in the synagogue: whom when Aquila and Priscilla had heard, they took him unto them, and expounded unto him the way of God more perfectly.
corruption_summary: Ministry is selected for by fluency, and Scripture gives the two founding communicators an impediment and a correction respectively.
corruption_paragraphs: Exodus 4:10-12 is God's answer to a man declining on grounds of communication: who hath made man's mouth? or who maketh the dumb, or deaf, or the seeing, or the blind? have not I the LORD? Now therefore go, and I will be with thy mouth, and teach thee what thou shalt say. The impediment is not denied or removed at that point; its authorship is claimed. Moses' objection was true and irrelevant.

Acts 18:24-26 is the counterpart. Apollos was eloquent and mighty in the scriptures, fervent in spirit, teaching diligently — and knowing only the baptism of John. Aquila and Priscilla heard him, took him unto them, and expounded unto him the way of God more perfectly. A gifted preacher was corrected by a couple who made tents, and the text records no resistance from him at all.
roots_summary: Hebrew ish debarim, a man of words — Moses' phrase; Greek logios (G3052), learned, eloquent — only of Apollos.
roots_lines: Hebrew ish debarim — a man of words; Exodus 4:10, I am not eloquent.
Greek logios (G3052) — eloquent, learned; only Acts 18:24.
Greek akribesteron (G199) — more perfectly; Acts 18:26, the correction he received.
usage: “I am not eloquent… but I am slow of speech” — true, and overruled.
“Who hath made man's mouth?” — authorship claimed rather than impediment removed.
“Expounded unto him the way of God more perfectly” — an eloquent man taught by tentmakers.

pos: v. (to clasp in the arms; rendering Hebrew chabaq)
etymology: From Latin in and brachium, arm. To embrace is to take into the arms — and Scripture's embraces mark reconciliations nobody expected.
biblical_def: To embrace is to clasp. Esau runs to meet Jacob, “and embraced him, and fell on his neck, and kissed him: and they wept” (Gen 33:4). Joseph falls on his brothers' necks (Gen 45:14–15). Ecclesiastes names “a time to embrace, and a time to refrain from embracing” (Ecc 3:5). Proverbs says of wisdom, “she shall be a crown of glory to thee… embrace her, and she shall promote thee” (Pro 4:8–9), and Paul embraces the Ephesian elders before sailing (Act 20:1 in the same gesture).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines embrace as to take, clasp or inclose in the arms; to press to the bosom in token of affection; to seize eagerly; to lay hold on; and to accept.
webster_full: EMBRACE, v.t. To take, clasp or inclose in the arms; to press to the bosom, in token of affection.
2. To seize eagerly; to lay hold on; to receive or take with willingness that which is offered.
3. To comprehend; to include or take in.
4. To comprise; to inclose; to encompass; to contain.
scriptures: Gen 33:4
And Esau ran to meet him, and embraced him, and fell on his neck, and kissed him: and they wept.
Ecc 3:5
A time to cast away stones, and a time to gather stones together; a time to embrace, and a time to refrain from embracing;
Pro 4:8
Exalt her, and she shall promote thee: she shall bring thee to honour, when thou dost embrace her.
And he fell upon his brother Benjamin's neck, and wept; and Benjamin wept upon his neck.
corruption_summary: Reconciliation is expected to require a negotiation, and Esau ran the distance and embraced the brother who had cheated him before a word was spoken.
corruption_paragraphs: Genesis 33:4 undoes twenty years of dread in one sentence: and Esau ran to meet him, and embraced him, and fell on his neck, and kissed him: and they wept. Jacob had divided his camp, sent waves of gifts ahead, and prepared a speech. None of it was needed. The wronged brother closed the distance at a run, and the reconciliation happened before Jacob delivered a single argument.

Ecclesiastes 3:5 supplies the discipline the gesture needs: a time to embrace, and a time to refrain from embracing. Affection has seasons and boundaries, and wisdom is knowing which is which. Proverbs 4:8 then puts the verb to a different object entirely — exalt her, and she shall promote thee: she shall bring thee to honour, when thou dost embrace her. Wisdom is to be held the way a person is held.
roots_summary: Hebrew chabaq (H2263), to clasp, embrace; naphal al tsavvar, to fall on the neck — the idiom of Genesis 33 and 45.
roots_lines: Hebrew chabaq (H2263) — to embrace; Genesis 33:4, 48:10, Ecclesiastes 3:5, Proverbs 4:8.
Hebrew nashaq (H5401) — to kiss; the companion action in Genesis 33:4.
Greek aspazomai (G782) — to greet, embrace; Acts 20:1, 21:6.
usage: “Esau ran to meet him, and embraced him” — before a word was spoken.
“A time to embrace, and a time to refrain from embracing” — affection has seasons.
“Embrace her, and she shall promote thee” — wisdom held like a person.

pos: v. (to put courage into; rendering Hebrew chazaq)
etymology: From en- and courage, from Latin cor, heart. To encourage is literally to put heart into someone — a transfer, not a compliment.
biblical_def: To encourage is to strengthen another's heart. Moses is told, “charge Joshua, and encourage him, and strengthen him: for he shall go over before this people” (Deu 3:28). David, at Ziklag with his men speaking of stoning him, “encouraged himself in the LORD his God” (1Sa 30:6). Hezekiah “spake comfortably” to the Levites (2Ch 30:22), and the builders of the idol encourage one another in Isaiah's satire (Isa 41:7).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines encourage as to give courage to; to give or increase confidence of success; to inspire with courage, spirit, or strength of mind; to embolden; to animate; to incite; to inspirit.
webster_full: ENCOURAGE, v.t. To give courage to; to give or increase confidence of success; to inspire with courage, spirit, or strength of mind; to embolden; to animate; to incite; to inspirit.
scriptures: Deu 3:28
But charge Joshua, and encourage him, and strengthen him: for he shall go over before this people, and he shall cause them to inherit the land which thou shalt see.

And David was greatly distressed; for the people spake of stoning him, because the soul of all the people was grieved, every man for his sons and for his daughters: but David encouraged himself in the LORD his God.

And Hezekiah spake comfortably unto all the Levites that taught the good knowledge of the LORD: and they did eat throughout the feast seven days, offering peace offerings, and making confession to the LORD God of their fathers.
Isa 41:7

So the carpenter encouraged the goldsmith, and he that smootheth with the hammer him that smote the anvil, saying, It is ready for the sodering: and he fastened it with nails, that it should not be moved.
corruption_summary: Encouragement is expected to arrive from someone else, and David at his lowest point encouraged himself in the LORD because there was no one left to do it.
corruption_paragraphs: 1 Samuel 30:6 is one of the loneliest verses in Scripture: and David was greatly distressed; for the people spake of stoning him, because the soul of all the people was grieved, every man for his sons and for his daughters: but David encouraged himself in the LORD his God. The city was burned, the families were taken, and his own men had turned. The encouragement had to come from a source none of them controlled, and the verse names it.

Deuteronomy 3:28 shows the other direction and its cost. Moses, told he will not enter the land, is commanded to charge Joshua, and encourage him, and strengthen him: for he shall go over before this people, and he shall cause them to inherit the land which thou shalt see. He is to put heart into the man who will finish what he cannot. That is a harder assignment than the leading was.
roots_summary: Hebrew chazaq (H2388), to be strong, to strengthen — the same verb in be strong and of a good courage; amets (H553), to be alert, courageous.
roots_lines: Hebrew chazaq (H2388) — to strengthen, encourage; Deuteronomy 3:28, 1:38, Isaiah 41:7.
Hebrew amets (H553) — to make strong, courageous; Deuteronomy 3:28.
Hebrew hithchazzeq — to strengthen oneself; 1 Samuel 30:6, David encouraged himself.
usage: “Encourage him, and strengthen him: for he shall go over” — Moses commissioning his successor.
“David encouraged himself in the LORD his God” — when no one else would.
“So the carpenter encouraged the goldsmith” — Isaiah's satire on idol-makers.

pos: n. (a cutter of stone or metal; rendering Hebrew charash)
etymology: From en- and grave, to carve. The engraver's work is permanent by design — which is why Scripture uses the craft for names God keeps.
biblical_def: An engraver cuts stone or metal. Bezaleel is filled with the Spirit “to devise cunning works… and in cutting of stones, to set them” (Exo 31:4–5), and Aholiab is named “an engraver, and a cunning workman” (Exo 38:23). The high priest's breastplate bore the tribes' names “with the work of an engraver in stone, like the engravings of a signet” (Exo 28:11,21). Zechariah promises, “I will engrave the graving thereof, saith the LORD of hosts” (Zec 3:9).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines engraver as a cutter of letters, figures or devices, on stone, metal or wood; one who engraves; a sculptor.
webster_full: ENGRAVER, n. A cutter of letters, figures or devices, on stone, metal or wood; one who engraves; a sculptor.
ENGRAVE, v.t. To cut, as metals, stones or other hard substances, with a chisel or graver.
scriptures: With the work of an engraver in stone, like the engravings of a signet, shalt thou engrave the two stones with the names of the children of Israel: thou shalt make them to be set in ouches of gold.

And the stones shall be with the names of the children of Israel, twelve, according to their names, like the engravings of a signet; every one with his name shall they be according to the twelve tribes.
And with him was Aholiab, son of Ahisamach, of the tribe of Dan, an engraver, and a cunning workman, and an embroiderer in blue, and in purple, and in scarlet, and fine linen.
Zec 3:9

For behold the stone that I have laid before Joshua; upon one stone shall be seven eyes: behold, I will engrave the graving thereof, saith the LORD of hosts, and I will remove the iniquity of that land in one day.
corruption_summary: Skilled craft is treated as decoration beside the real work of ministry, and Exodus names the engraver as the first man in Scripture said to be filled with the Spirit of God.
corruption_paragraphs: Exodus 31:3 is the first occurrence in the Bible of a man being filled with the Spirit of God, and the man is a craftsman: I have filled him with the spirit of God, in wisdom, and in understanding, and in knowledge, and in all manner of workmanship, to devise cunning works… and in cutting of stones. Design, metalwork, and engraving are named as Spirit-given competencies before any prophet or priest is so described.

The engraver's most consequential job was the breastplate: the names of the children of Israel, twelve, according to their names, like the engravings of a signet; every one with his name. Aaron carried those cut names over his heart whenever he went into the holy place. Engraving was chosen because it does not wear off — and Isaiah later has God say, Behold, I have graven thee upon the palms of my hands.
roots_summary: Hebrew charash (H2796), a craftsman in stone, wood, or metal; pittuach (H6603), engraving; chotham (H2368), a signet.
roots_lines: Hebrew charash (H2796) — engraver, craftsman; Exodus 28:11, 38:23.
Hebrew pittuach (H6603) — engraving, carved work; Exodus 28:11, 21, 36, Zechariah 3:9.
Hebrew chotham (H2368) — signet, seal; like the engravings of a signet.
usage: “With the work of an engraver in stone, like the engravings of a signet” — the breastplate names.
“I have filled him with the spirit of God… in all manner of workmanship” — the first filling recorded.
“I will engrave the graving thereof” — God taking up the craft.

pos: v. (to draw by allurement; rendering Hebrew pathah, Greek deleazo)
etymology: From Old French enticier, to provoke. The Greek deleazo is a fisherman's word — to bait a hook.
biblical_def: To entice is to draw by allurement. Proverbs opens with the warning: “My son, if sinners entice thee, consent thou not” (Pro 1:10). James locates the mechanism inside the man: “every man is tempted, when he is drawn away of his own lust, and enticed” (Jas 1:14). Deuteronomy legislates against a family member who entices secretly to other gods (Deu 13:6), and Peter describes false teachers “beguiling unstable souls” (2Pe 2:14).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines entice as to incite or instigate, by exciting hope or desire; usually in a bad sense; to allure; to attract; to draw by blandishments or persuasions.
webster_full: ENTICE, v.t. To incite or instigate, by exciting hope or desire; usually in a bad sense.
2. To allure; to attract; to draw by blandishments or persuasions, as by exciting hope or desire of pleasure or advantage.
scriptures: Pro 1:10
My son, if sinners entice thee, consent thou not.
Jas 1:14
But every man is tempted, when he is drawn away of his own lust, and enticed.
Deu 13:6

If thy brother, the son of thy mother, or thy son, or thy daughter, or the wife of thy bosom, or thy friend, which is as thine own soul, entice thee secretly, saying, Let us go and serve other gods, which thou hast not known, thou, nor thy fathers;
Having eyes full of adultery, and that cannot cease from sin; beguiling unstable souls: an heart they have exercised with covetous practices; cursed children:
corruption_summary: Temptation is blamed on the tempter, and James says the bait only works because it matches an appetite already present.
corruption_paragraphs: James 1:14 removes the usual excuse without removing responsibility from the tempter: every man is tempted, when he is drawn away of his own lust, and enticed. The bait is external; the hunger is not. That is why the same enticement fails on one man and lands on another, and why the remedy is not merely avoiding baited hooks but dealing with what makes them attractive. James has just insisted God tempts no man, which closes the other escape route.

Proverbs 1:10 gives the shortest complete instruction in the book: my son, if sinners entice thee, consent thou not. Two clauses — the enticement is assumed as certain, and the response is a single word. What follows is a description of the pitch itself, cast us in thy lot; let us all have one purse, which is the promise of belonging rather than of pleasure. Most enticement is an offer of company.
roots_summary: Hebrew pathah (H6601), to be open, to entice or persuade; Greek deleazo (G1185), to bait a hook, entice.
roots_lines: Hebrew pathah (H6601) — to entice, persuade; Proverbs 1:10, Judges 14:15, 16:5 of Delilah.
Greek deleazo (G1185) — to entice with bait; James 1:14, 2 Peter 2:14, 18.
Greek epithumia (G1939) — lust, desire; James 1:14, his own lust.
usage: “If sinners entice thee, consent thou not” — the shortest complete instruction.
“Drawn away of his own lust, and enticed” — the hunger is not external.
“Let us all have one purse” — the pitch is belonging, not pleasure.

pos: v. (made a stranger; rendering Hebrew zur and nazar)
etymology: From Latin extraneus, foreign. To be estranged is to have become foreign to what one belonged to — a relation broken from within.
biblical_def: To be estranged is to be made a stranger. The psalmist says the wicked “are estranged from the womb: they go astray as soon as they be born, speaking lies” (Psa 58:3). Job complains that his acquaintance are verily estranged from him (Job 19:13). Ezekiel says Israel is “estranged from me through their idols” (Eze 14:5), and Jeremiah charges that they have “estranged this place” and filled it with the blood of innocents (Jer 19:4).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines estrange as to keep at a distance; to withdraw; to cease to frequent and be familiar with; to alienate, as the affections; and to divert from its original use or possessor.
webster_full: ESTRANGE, v.t. To keep at a distance; to withdraw; to cease to frequent and be familiar with.
2. To alienate, as the affections.
3. To divert from its original use or possessor; to apply to a purpose foreign from its original.
scriptures: Psa 58:3
The wicked are estranged from the womb: they go astray as soon as they be born, speaking lies.
He hath put my brethren far from me, and mine acquaintance are verily estranged from me.
Eze 14:5
That I may take the house of Israel in their own heart, because they are all estranged from me through their idols.
Jer 19:4

Because they have forsaken me, and have estranged this place, and have burned incense in it unto other gods, whom neither they nor their fathers have known, nor the kings of Judah, and have filled this place with the blood of innocents;
corruption_summary: Estrangement from God is imagined as a drift that happened to someone, and Ezekiel names the mechanism — estranged from me through their idols.
corruption_paragraphs: Ezekiel 14:5 traces estrangement to a cause and locates it inside: they are all estranged from me through their idols. The chapter opens with elders of Israel sitting before the prophet to enquire of the LORD, and God's answer is that these men have set up their idols in their heart. Nothing was in their hands; the idols were internal, and the estrangement they produced was real enough that God declines to be enquired of by them.

Psalm 58:3 pushes the origin further back than anyone finds comfortable: the wicked are estranged from the womb: they go astray as soon as they be born. This is not a claim about particular infants but about the race's condition, and it is the same doctrine David states in Psalm 51 about himself. Estrangement, in Scripture's account, is not first a decision but an inheritance — which is why the remedy has to be a new birth rather than a better resolution.
roots_summary: Hebrew zur (H2114), to be a stranger, estranged; nazar (H5144), to separate oneself; Greek apallotrioo (G526), to alienate.
roots_lines: Hebrew zur (H2114) — to be estranged, a stranger; Psalm 58:3, 78:30, Job 19:13.
Hebrew nazar (H5144) — to separate; Ezekiel 14:5, 7, estranged from me through their idols.
Hebrew nakar (H5234) — to be foreign; Jeremiah 19:4, they have estranged this place.
usage: “Estranged from me through their idols” — the mechanism named.
“Estranged from the womb” — an inheritance, not first a decision.
“Mine acquaintance are verily estranged from me” — Job's losses.

pos: adj. (plainly seen; rendering Greek delos and prodelos)
etymology: From Latin evidens, seen out. Evident names what cannot be missed — and Paul uses it for both the works of the flesh and the failure of law-keeping.
biblical_def: Evident means plainly seen. Paul says, “the works of the flesh are manifest” and lists them (Gal 5:19), and elsewhere, “that no man is justified by the law in the sight of God, it is evident” (Gal 3:11). Hebrews argues, “it is yet far more evident: for that after the similitude of Melchisedec there ariseth another priest” (Heb 7:15). Paul tells the Philippians their fearlessness is “an evident token of perdition” to their adversaries but of salvation to them (Php 1:28).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines evident as open to be seen; clear to the mental eye; apparent; manifest; plain; obvious; conspicuous.
webster_full: EVIDENT, a. Open to be seen; clear to the mental eye; apparent; manifest; plain; obvious; conspicuous.
scriptures: Gal 3:11
But that no man is justified by the law in the sight of God, it is evident: for, The just shall live by faith.
Gal 5:19
Now the works of the flesh are manifest, which are these; Adultery, fornication, uncleanness, lasciviousness,
Php 1:28
And in nothing terrified by your adversaries: which is to them an evident token of perdition, but to you of salvation, and that of God.
Heb 7:15
And it is yet far more evident: for that after the similitude of Melchisedec there ariseth another priest,
corruption_summary: Doctrine is treated as inherently obscure, and Paul repeatedly says the decisive things are evident — visible to anyone willing to look.
corruption_paragraphs: Galatians 3:11 makes an appeal to plainness rather than to authority: but that no man is justified by the law in the sight of God, it is evident: for, The just shall live by faith. Paul's argument is that the Old Testament itself says so and always did. He is not introducing a novelty against a settled reading; he is claiming the settled reading was there in Habakkuk all along and anyone can check.

Philippians 1:28 shows evidence working in two directions at once: in nothing terrified by your adversaries: which is to them an evident token of perdition, but to you of salvation, and that of God. The same courage under pressure is read by opponents as a sign of their own peril and by the church as a sign of God's keeping. Nothing about the behaviour changes; the reading of it differs entirely with the reader.
roots_summary: Greek delos (G1212), clear, evident; prodelos (G4271), evident beforehand; endeixis (G1732), a token or proof.
roots_lines: Greek delos (G1212) — evident, manifest; Galatians 3:11, 1 Corinthians 15:27.
Greek prodelos (G4271) — evident beforehand; Hebrews 7:14-15, 1 Timothy 5:24-25.
Greek endeixis (G1732) — token, evidence; Philippians 1:28, Romans 3:25.
usage: “No man is justified by the law… it is evident” — an appeal to plainness.
“An evident token of perdition, but to you of salvation” — the same courage read two ways.
“It is yet far more evident” — Hebrews building its case.

pos: v. (to surpass; rendering Hebrew yathar, Greek perisseuo)
etymology: From Latin excellere, to rise above. Excellence in Scripture is commended, and its direction is always specified.
biblical_def: To excel is to surpass. Paul redirects the Corinthians' ambition: “even so ye, forasmuch as ye are zealous of spiritual gifts, seek that ye may excel to the edifying of the church” (1Co 14:12). Jacob says of Reuben, “Unstable as water, thou shalt not excel” (Gen 49:4). The psalmist calls angels “ye his angels, that excel in strength” (Psa 103:20), and Proverbs says of the virtuous woman, “many daughters have done virtuously, but thou excellest them all” (Pro 31:29).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines excel as to go beyond; to exceed; to surpass in good qualities or laudable deeds; to outdo; and to exceed or go beyond in bad qualities or deeds.
webster_full: EXCEL, v.t. To go beyond; to exceed; to surpass in good qualities or laudable deeds; to outdo.
2. To exceed or go beyond in bad qualities or deeds.
EXCEL, v.i. To have good qualities, or to perform meritorious actions, in an unusual degree; to be eminent, illustrious, or distinguished.
scriptures: Even so ye, forasmuch as ye are zealous of spiritual gifts, seek that ye may excel to the edifying of the church.
Gen 49:4
Unstable as water, thou shalt not excel; because thou wentest up to thy father's bed; then defiledst thou it: he went up to my couch. thou
Bless the LORD, ye his angels, that excel in strength, that do his commandments, hearkening unto the voice of his word.
Many daughters have done virtuously, but thou excellest them all.
corruption_summary: Excellence is pursued for its own sake, and Paul redirects a church's genuine zeal by specifying what it should excel at — the edifying of the church.
corruption_paragraphs: 1 Corinthians 14:12 does not dampen ambition; it aims it: even so ye, forasmuch as ye are zealous of spiritual gifts, seek that ye may excel to the edifying of the church. Paul grants the zeal as real and good, then attaches a target that removes the competitive element entirely. A man competing to build others up is not competing with them. The whole chapter's argument about tongues and prophecy follows from that single redirection.

Genesis 49:4 shows excellence forfeited rather than lacked: unstable as water, thou shalt not excel. Reuben was the firstborn, with the birthright in hand, and Jacob's verdict names the reason — instability. Not weakness, not lack of gifting. What disqualified him was that nothing about him could be relied upon twice, and the blessing passed to others.
roots_summary: Hebrew yathar (H3498), to exceed, remain over; gibbor koach, mighty in strength — of the angels; Greek perisseuo (G4052), to abound, excel.
roots_lines: Greek perisseuo (G4052) — to abound, excel; 1 Corinthians 14:12, 2 Corinthians 8:7.
Hebrew yathar (H3498) — to excel, exceed; Genesis 49:4, Proverbs 31:29.
Greek oikodome (G3619) — edifying, building up; the target Paul assigns.
usage: “Seek that ye may excel to the edifying of the church” — ambition aimed, not dampened.
“Unstable as water, thou shalt not excel” — excellence forfeited by unreliability.
“Thou excellest them all” — the husband's verdict in Proverbs 31.

pos: n. (going beyond measure; rendering Greek asotia)
etymology: From Latin excedere, to go out beyond. Excess names a boundary crossed, and Paul sets it against being filled with the Spirit.
biblical_def: Excess is going beyond measure. Paul's contrast is exact: “be not drunk with wine, wherein is excess; but be filled with the Spirit” (Eph 5:18). Peter says the past sufficed for walking in “excess of wine, revellings, banquetings”, and notes that former companions think it strange that you run not with them “to the same excess of riot” (1Pe 4:3–4). Christ says the Pharisees' cups are clean without and within are full of extortion and excess (Mat 23:25).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines excess as literally, a going beyond; hence, any transgression of due limits; superfluity; that which is beyond necessity or wants; and intemperance in eating or drinking.
webster_full: EXCESS, n. Literally, a going beyond; hence, any transgression of due limits.
2. Superfluity; that which is beyond necessity or wants; as an excess of provisions.
3. That which is beyond the common measure, proportion, or due quantity.
4. Superabundance of any thing.
5. Any transgression of due limits; intemperance in eating or drinking.
scriptures: Eph 5:18
And be not drunk with wine, wherein is excess; but be filled with the Spirit;
For the time past of our life may suffice us to have wrought the will of the Gentiles, when we walked in lasciviousness, lusts, excess of wine, revellings, banquetings, and abominable idolatries:
Wherein they think it strange that ye run not with them to the same excess of riot, speaking evil of you:
Woe unto you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! for ye make clean the outside of the cup and of the platter, but within they are full of extortion and excess.
corruption_summary: Sobriety is presented as the removal of a pleasure, and Paul offers it as a substitution — not drunk with wine, but filled with the Spirit.
corruption_paragraphs: Ephesians 5:18 is a substitution rather than a prohibition: be not drunk with wine, wherein is excess; but be filled with the Spirit. The two clauses are parallel because both describe being under an influence that governs speech and behaviour. What follows names the results — speaking to yourselves in psalms and hymns, singing and making melody, giving thanks always, submitting yourselves one to another. The alternative to one filling is another, not emptiness.

1 Peter 4:4 records the social cost with unusual sympathy for the convert: wherein they think it strange that ye run not with them to the same excess of riot, speaking evil of you. Peter does not promise the old company will understand. He says they will find the change strange and will speak against it, and he tells believers to expect that rather than to explain themselves out of it.
roots_summary: Greek asotia (G810), riotous excess, unsavedness — the word for the prodigal's living; akrasia (G192), lack of self-control, in Matthew 23:25.
roots_lines: Greek asotia (G810) — excess, riot; Ephesians 5:18, Titus 1:6, 1 Peter 4:4.
Greek akrasia (G192) — incontinence, excess; Matthew 23:25, 1 Corinthians 7:5.
Greek pleroo (G4137) — to fill; Ephesians 5:18, be filled with the Spirit.
usage: “Be not drunk with wine… but be filled with the Spirit” — a substitution, not a subtraction.
“They think it strange that ye run not with them” — the social cost, expected.
“Within they are full of extortion and excess” — the clean cup.

pos: n., v. (a plea offered to avoid; rendering Greek paraiteomai and anapologetos)
etymology: From Latin excusare, to free from a charge. An excuse is an offered reason — and Scripture examines several and accepts none.
biblical_def: An excuse is a plea to be released. Christ's parable records three in a row: “they all with one consent began to make excuse” — a field, five yoke of oxen, and a wife (Luk 14:18–20). Paul says creation leaves men “without excuse” (Rom 1:20), and again of the moralizer, “therefore thou art inexcusable, O man” (Rom 2:1). Adam's first response to God is an excuse that implicates both his wife and his Maker (Gen 3:12).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines excuse as a plea offered in extenuation of a fault or irregular deportment; apology; and that which excuses, that which extenuates or justifies a fault.
webster_full: EXCUSE, v.t. To pardon; to free from the imputation of fault or blame; to acquit of guilt.
2. To pardon, as a fault; to forgive entirely, or to admit to be little censurable.
3. To free from an obligation or duty.
EXCUSE, n. A plea offered in extenuation of a fault or irregular deportment; apology.
scriptures: And they all with one consent began to make excuse. The first said unto him, I have bought a piece of ground, and I must needs go and see it: I pray thee have me excused.
Rom 1:20
For the invisible things of him from the creation of the world are clearly seen, being understood by the things that are made, even his eternal power and Godhead; so that they are without excuse:
Rom 2:1
Therefore thou art inexcusable, O man, whosoever thou art that judgest: for wherein thou judgest another, thou condemnest thyself; for thou that judgest doest the same things.
Gen 3:12
And the man said, The woman whom thou gavest to be with me, she gave me of the tree, and I did eat.
corruption_summary: Excuses are offered as though sincerity settled the matter, and every excuse in Luke 14 was true, reasonable, and fatal.
corruption_paragraphs: Luke 14:18-20 is careful to make the excuses good ones. A purchased field must be inspected; new oxen must be proved; a newly married man had a legal exemption from military service. None of the three is a lie, and none of them is trivial. That is what makes the parable so uncomfortable — the invitation was declined by reasonable men with genuine commitments, and the master's response was anger and a guest list drawn from the streets.

Genesis 3:12 records the first excuse ever offered and its structure has not improved since: the woman whom thou gavest to be with me, she gave me of the tree, and I did eat. Two parties are implicated before the confession arrives, and the confession itself is three words long. Adam's answer is technically accurate in every particular, which is precisely why Scripture treats accuracy as an insufficient defence.
roots_summary: Greek paraiteomai (G3868), to beg off, excuse oneself; anapologetos (G379), without excuse, indefensible.
roots_lines: Greek paraiteomai (G3868) — to make excuse, beg off; Luke 14:18-19.
Greek anapologetos (G379) — without excuse; Romans 1:20, 2:1.
Greek prophasis (G4392) — a pretext, cloke; John 15:22, now they have no cloke for their sin.
usage: “They all with one consent began to make excuse” — three good reasons, all fatal.
“So that they are without excuse” — the verdict on creation's testimony.
“The woman whom thou gavest to be with me” — the first excuse, technically accurate.

pos: adj. (skilled by experience; rendering Hebrew chanak, Greek gnostes)
etymology: From Latin experiri, to try. An expert is one taught by trial rather than by instruction — skill proved in use.
biblical_def: Expert means skilled by experience. Chronicles describes David's men of Zebulun as “expert in war, with all instruments of war… which could keep rank: they were not of double heart” (1Ch 12:33). Solomon's servants are “expert in wood” (2Ch 2:8 in the same idiom). Paul tells Agrippa, “I know thee to be expert in all customs and questions which are among the Jews” (Act 26:3), and Jeremiah says the northern army are “mighty men… expert in war” (Jer 50:9 in the same phrase).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines expert as properly, experienced; taught by use, practice or experience; hence, skilful; well instructed; having familiar knowledge of; dextrous; adroit.
webster_full: EXPERT, a. Properly, experienced; taught by use, practice or experience; hence, skilful; well instructed; having familiar knowledge of.
2. Dextrous; adroit; ready; prompt; having a facility of operation or performance from practice.
scriptures: Of Zebulun, such as went forth to battle, expert in war, with all instruments of war, fifty thousand, which could keep rank: they were not of double heart.
Act 26:3
Especially because I know thee to be expert in all customs and questions which are among the Jews: wherefore I beseech thee to hear me patiently.

And of the children of Issachar, which were men that had understanding of the times, to know what Israel ought to do; the heads of them were two hundred; and all their brethren were at their commandment.
Jer 50:9

For, lo, I will raise and cause to come up against Babylon an assembly of great nations from the north country: and they shall set themselves in array against her; from thence she shall be taken: their arrows shall be as of a mighty expert man; none shall return in vain.
corruption_summary: Expertise is credited to knowledge, and Chronicles pairs it with two things knowledge does not supply — the ability to keep rank, and an undivided heart.
corruption_paragraphs: 1 Chronicles 12:33 lists three qualities together and only one is technical: expert in war, with all instruments of war, fifty thousand, which could keep rank: they were not of double heart. Skill with weapons, the discipline to hold formation, and singleness of heart. An expert who cannot keep rank is a liability, and one of divided loyalty is worse. The chapter's most famous line concerns their neighbours — the men of Issachar, which were men that had understanding of the times, to know what Israel ought to do.

Acts 26:3 shows Paul granting a hostile authority genuine credit: I know thee to be expert in all customs and questions which are among the Jews: wherefore I beseech thee to hear me patiently. He is on trial before a king who could condemn him, and he opens by acknowledging Agrippa's real competence. Flattery it is not; the assessment was accurate, and Paul used it as the ground for asking a hearing rather than as a bid for favour.
roots_summary: Hebrew arak milchamah, to set in battle array; lo leb valeb, not of a heart and a heart — the idiom for undivided; Greek gnostes (G1109), one who knows.
roots_lines: Hebrew arak (H6186) — to arrange, set in order; 1 Chronicles 12:33, expert in war.
Hebrew leb valeb — a heart and a heart; 1 Chronicles 12:33, not of double heart.
Greek gnostes (G1109) — an expert, knower; only Acts 26:3.
usage: “Expert in war… which could keep rank: they were not of double heart” — three qualities, one technical.
“I know thee to be expert in all customs” — credit granted to a hostile judge.
“Men that had understanding of the times” — the neighbouring tribe's expertise.

pos: v. (to lift up in praise; rendering Hebrew rum and salal)
etymology: From Latin extollere, to lift out or up. To extol is literally to raise — praise pictured as elevation.
biblical_def: To extol is to lift up in praise. David resolves, “I will extol thee, my God, O king; and I will bless thy name for ever and ever” (Psa 145:1). Psalm 30 gives the reason: “I will extol thee, O LORD; for thou hast lifted me up, and hast not made my foes to rejoice over me” (Psa 30:1). Isaiah applies the verb to the Servant: “behold, my servant shall deal prudently, he shall be exalted and extolled, and be very high” (Isa 52:13). Nebuchadnezzar, restored, extols the King of heaven (Dan 4:37).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines extol as to raise in words or eulogy; to praise; to exalt in commendation; to magnify.
webster_full: EXTOL, v.t. To raise in words or eulogy; to praise; to exalt in commendation; to magnify.
We extol virtues, noble exploits, and heroism.
scriptures: David's Psalm of praise. I will extol thee, my God, O king; and I will bless thy name for ever and ever.
Psa 30:1
A Psalm and Song at the dedication of the house of David. I will extol thee, O LORD; for thou hast lifted me up, and hast not made my foes to rejoice over me.
Behold, my servant shall deal prudently, he shall be exalted and extolled, and be very high.
Dan 4:37
Now I Nebuchadnezzar praise and extol and honour the King of heaven, all whose works are truth, and his ways judgment: and those that walk in pride he is able to abase.
corruption_summary: Praise is offered when circumstances warrant it, and Psalm 30 extols God for a lifting that had already happened rather than for one requested.
corruption_paragraphs: Psalm 30:1 supplies its own reason and the verb is repeated in both directions: I will extol thee, O LORD; for thou hast lifted me up. The psalmist raises God because God raised him. That is the ordinary logic of biblical praise — it is response rather than technique, and it looks backward at something done before it looks forward at something wanted.

Daniel 4:37 is the most unexpected doxology in Scripture because of who says it: Now I Nebuchadnezzar praise and extol and honour the King of heaven, all whose works are truth, and his ways judgment: and those that walk in pride he is able to abase. A pagan emperor who had been reduced to eating grass ends his own chapter with a sentence about pride that he had learned from the inside.
roots_summary: Hebrew rum (H7311), to be high, to exalt; salal (H5549), to lift up, cast up a highway; Aramaic rum in Daniel 4:37.
roots_lines: Hebrew rum (H7311) — to exalt, extol; Psalm 30:1, 145:1, Isaiah 52:13.
Hebrew salal (H5549) — to lift up, extol; Psalm 68:4, extol him that rideth upon the heavens.
Aramaic rum (H7313) — to exalt; Daniel 4:37, praise and extol and honour.
usage: “I will extol thee… for thou hast lifted me up” — praise as response.
“He shall be exalted and extolled, and be very high” — the Servant's outcome stated first.
“Now I Nebuchadnezzar praise and extol” — a lesson learned from the inside.

pos: adj. (without faith; rendering Greek apistos)
etymology: Faith with the privative ending. The Greek apistos covers both unbelieving and untrustworthy — a useful ambiguity.
biblical_def: Faithless means without faith. Christ says it twice at moments of failure: “O faithless and perverse generation, how long shall I be with you? how long shall I suffer you?” (Mat 17:17), and to Thomas, “be not faithless, but believing” (Joh 20:27). Proverbs says, “Confidence in an unfaithful man in time of trouble is like a broken tooth” (Pro 25:19), and Jeremiah repeatedly addresses faithless Israel.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines faithless as disbelieving; not believing; and not adhering to allegiance or covenants; not true to one's promise; perfidious; treacherous.
webster_full: FAITHLESS, a. Without faith; disbelieving; not believing.
2. Not adhering to allegiance, or duty; disloyal; perfidious; treacherous.
3. Not true to one's promise or covenant; not observant of promises.
4. Deceptive; not to be relied on.
scriptures: Then Jesus answered and said, O faithless and perverse generation, how long shall I be with you? how long shall I suffer you? bring him hither to me.
Then saith he to Thomas, Reach hither thy finger, and behold my hands; and reach hither thy hand, and thrust it into my side: and be not faithless, but believing.
Confidence in an unfaithful man in time of trouble is like a broken tooth, and a foot out of joint.
Jesus saith unto him, Thomas, because thou hast seen me, thou hast believed: blessed are they that have not seen, and yet have believed.
corruption_summary: Doubt is treated as either shameful or admirable, and Christ handles Thomas by neither shaming him nor commending him — He supplies the evidence and issues a command.
corruption_paragraphs: John 20:27 is remarkable for what Christ does with a stated condition. Thomas had specified exactly what he required — the print of the nails, the hand in the side — and Christ arrives and offers precisely that, quoting the man's own terms back to him. Then the command: be not faithless, but believing. The evidence is given and belief is still commanded; the sight did not do the work by itself.

The next verse guards the rest of us: blessed are they that have not seen, and yet have believed. That is not a rebuke of Thomas, who is left in the room as a believer confessing my Lord and my God. It is a word to every reader who will never get the offer Thomas got, and John says two verses later that he wrote his Gospel so that they might believe without it.
roots_summary: Greek apistos (G571), unbelieving, faithless; apistia (G570), unbelief; pistos (G4103), faithful, believing.
roots_lines: Greek apistos (G571) — faithless, unbelieving; Matthew 17:17, John 20:27, 1 Corinthians 6:6.
Greek pistos (G4103) — believing, faithful; John 20:27, the alternative commanded.
Hebrew bagad (H898) — to deal treacherously; Proverbs 25:19, an unfaithful man.
usage: “O faithless and perverse generation” — said at the foot of the mount.
“Be not faithless, but believing” — evidence given, belief still commanded.
“Blessed are they that have not seen, and yet have believed” — a word for the rest.

pos: n., adj. (without a father; rendering Hebrew yathom)
etymology: Father with the privative ending. The fatherless in Israel's law are a protected class, and God repeatedly names Himself their relative.
biblical_def: The fatherless are those without a father. God takes the title personally: “A father of the fatherless, and a judge of the widows, is God in his holy habitation” (Psa 68:5). The law forbids afflicting them and attaches a terrible warning (Exo 22:22–24). Deuteronomy leaves the forgotten sheaf and the gleanings for them (Deu 24:19–21), and James defines religion by them: “Pure religion and undefiled before God and the Father is this, To visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction” (Jas 1:27).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines fatherless as destitute of a living father; as a fatherless child; and without a known author.
webster_full: FATHERLESS, a. Destitute of a living father; as a fatherless child.
2. Without a known author.
FATHERLESSNESS, n. The state of being without a father.
scriptures: Psa 68:5
A father of the fatherless, and a judge of the widows, is God in his holy habitation.
Ye shall not afflict any widow, or fatherless child.
Jas 1:27
Pure religion and undefiled before God and the Father is this, To visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction, and to keep himself unspotted from the world.

When thou cuttest down thine harvest in thy field, and hast forgot a sheaf in the field, thou shalt not go again to fetch it: it shall be for the stranger, for the fatherless, and for the widow: that the LORD thy God may bless thee in all the work of thine hands.
corruption_summary: Care for the fatherless is treated as one charitable option among many, and James makes it half of the definition of undefiled religion.
corruption_paragraphs: James 1:27 does not say visiting the fatherless is a good work; it says it is what pure religion is: pure religion and undefiled before God and the Father is this, To visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction, and to keep himself unspotted from the world. Two halves, and neither is optional. A community rigorous about the second half and absent on the first has kept half a definition and called it obedience.

Psalm 68:5 explains why the duty is so heavily weighted: a father of the fatherless, and a judge of the widows, is God in his holy habitation. God does not merely command care for them; He identifies Himself by the relation. Exodus 22:23-24 states the consequence with unusual heat — if thou afflict them in any wise, and they cry at all unto me, I will surely hear their cry; and my wrath shall wax hot.
roots_summary: Hebrew yathom (H3490), an orphan, fatherless; Greek orphanos (G3737), orphan — the word Christ uses in John 14:18, I will not leave you comfortless.
roots_lines: Hebrew yathom (H3490) — fatherless, orphan; Exodus 22:22, Deuteronomy 24:19-21, Psalm 68:5.
Greek orphanos (G3737) — orphan, comfortless; James 1:27, John 14:18.
Hebrew almanah (H490) — widow; the constant companion term.
usage: “A father of the fatherless… is God in his holy habitation” — the relation claimed.
“To visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction” — half the definition of religion.
“My wrath shall wax hot” — the consequence of afflicting them.

pos: adj. (renowned; rendering Hebrew shem, a name)
etymology: From Latin fama, report. The Hebrew idiom is men of name — renown as a name that travels ahead of a person.
biblical_def: Famous means renowned. Genesis says of the pre-flood world, “there were giants in the earth in those days… mighty men which were of old, men of renown” (Gen 6:4). Numbers calls Korah's company “famous in the congregation, men of renown” before the earth swallowed them (Num 16:2). Ruth's neighbours bless Boaz, “do thou worthily in Ephratah, and be famous in Bethlehem” (Rut 4:11), and the psalmist says of the temple's destroyers, “A man was famous according as he had lifted up axes upon the thick trees” (Psa 74:5).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines famous as celebrated in fame or public report; renowned; much talked of and praised; distinguished in story.
webster_full: FAMOUS, a. Celebrated in fame or public report; renowned; much talked of and praised; distinguished in story.
2. Sometimes in a bad sense; notorious.
scriptures: Gen 6:4

There were giants in the earth in those days; and also after that, when the sons of God came in unto the daughters of men, and they bare children to them, the same became mighty men which were of old, men of renown.
Num 16:2
And they rose up before Moses, with certain of the children of Israel, two hundred and fifty princes of the assembly, famous in the congregation, men of renown:
Rut 4:11

And all the people that were in the gate, and the elders, said, We are witnesses. The LORD make the woman that is come into thine house like Rachel and like Leah, which two did build the house of Israel: and do thou worthily in Ephratah, and be famous in Bethlehem: do
Psa 74:5
A man was famous according as he had lifted up axes upon the thick trees.
corruption_summary: Renown is treated as evidence of worth, and Numbers 16 introduces the men who led the rebellion as famous in the congregation.
corruption_paragraphs: Numbers 16:2 names the credentials before the catastrophe: they rose up before Moses, with certain of the children of Israel, two hundred and fifty princes of the assembly, famous in the congregation, men of renown. These were not marginal malcontents. They were the recognized leadership, and the chapter records the ground opening under them. Fame within a religious community is not a certificate of standing before God.

Ruth 4:11 shows the word used well, and the blessing is domestic: the LORD make the woman that is come into thine house like Rachel and like Leah… and do thou worthily in Ephratah, and be famous in Bethlehem. Boaz's renown is wished for him in a village, attached to worthy conduct and a marriage. Three generations later that village produced David, and the blessing was answered more largely than anyone standing in the gate could have known.
roots_summary: Hebrew shem (H8034), name, renown — the idiom anshe hashem, men of the name; qara shem, to call a name, in Ruth 4:11.
roots_lines: Hebrew anshe hashem — men of renown; Genesis 6:4, Numbers 16:2.
Hebrew shem (H8034) — name, fame; Ruth 4:11, 14, Genesis 11:4, let us make us a name.
Hebrew yada (H3045) — to be known; Psalm 74:5 in the sense of being noticed.
usage: “Famous in the congregation, men of renown” — introduced before the ground opened.
“Be famous in Bethlehem” — renown wished in a village, answered in David.
“Men of renown” — the pre-flood world's estimate of itself.

pos: v. (to pretend; rendering Hebrew nakar and shaqar)
etymology: From Latin fingere, to shape or invent. To feign is to manufacture an appearance — the same root that gives us fiction.
biblical_def: To feign is to pretend. David feigns madness before Achish (1Sa 21:13). Joab sends a wise woman of Tekoah to Absalom's father, telling her to “feign thyself to be a mourner” (2Sa 14:2). Jeroboam's wife is told to feign herself another woman before the blind prophet Ahijah, who names her at the door (1Ki 14:2,5–6). Christ's enemies “sent forth spies, which should feign themselves just men” (Luk 20:20), and Jeremiah says Judah returned “feignedly” (Jer 3:10).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines feign as to invent or imagine; to form an idea or conception of something not real; to make a show of, to pretend; to assume a false appearance; and to dissemble.
webster_full: FEIGN, v.t. To invent or imagine; to form an idea or conception of something not real.
2. To make a show of; to pretend; to assume a false appearance; to counterfeit.
3. To represent falsely; to pretend; to form and relate a fictitious tale.
4. To dissemble; to conceal.
scriptures: And the LORD said unto Ahijah, Behold, the wife of Jeroboam cometh to ask a thing of thee for her son; for he is sick: thus and thus shalt thou say unto her: for it shall be, when she cometh in, that she shall feign herself to be another woman.

And it was so, when Ahijah heard the sound of her feet, as she came in at the door, that he said, Come in, thou wife of Jeroboam; why feignest thou thyself to be another? for I am sent to thee with heavy tidings.

And they watched him, and sent forth spies, which should feign themselves just men, that they might take hold of his words, that so they might deliver him unto the power and authority of the governor.
Jer 3:10
And yet for all this her treacherous sister Judah hath not turned unto me with her whole heart, but feignedly, saith the LORD.
corruption_summary: Pretence is trusted because it usually works, and 1 Kings has a blind prophet greet a disguised queen by name at the door.
corruption_paragraphs: 1 Kings 14 is a study in the futility of disguise. Jeroboam sends his wife in disguise to a prophet who cannot see, and God tells Ahijah in advance: behold, the wife of Jeroboam cometh to ask a thing of thee for her son; for he is sick: thus and thus shalt thou say unto her: for it shall be, when she cometh in, that she shall feign herself to be another woman. She arrives, and before she speaks he calls out: Come in, thou wife of Jeroboam; why feignest thou thyself to be another?

Jeremiah 3:10 applies the word to national repentance, which is the most dangerous place for it: and yet for all this her treacherous sister Judah hath not turned unto me with her whole heart, but feignedly, saith the LORD. A reform had actually happened — Josiah's — with real reforms and real ceremonies. God's assessment was that the turning was performed rather than made, and the exile followed anyway.
roots_summary: Hebrew nakar (H5234), to act as a stranger, disguise; shaqar (H8267), falsehood — feignedly is literally in falsehood; Greek hupokrinomai (G5271), to play a part.
roots_lines: Hebrew nakar (H5234) — to disguise, feign; 1 Kings 14:5-6.
Hebrew sheqer (H8267) — falsehood; Jeremiah 3:10, but feignedly.
Greek hupokrinomai (G5271) — to act a part, feign; only Luke 20:20.
usage: “Why feignest thou thyself to be another?” — the blind prophet at the door.
“Which should feign themselves just men” — the spies sent to trap Christ.
“Not… with her whole heart, but feignedly” — a real reform, performed.

pos: n. (one serving the same master; rendering Greek sundoulos)
etymology: Fellow with servant. The Greek sundoulos is a slave alongside another slave — equality established by a shared owner.
biblical_def: A fellowservant serves the same master. The unmerciful servant seizes one: “the same servant went out, and found one of his fellowservants, which owed him an hundred pence” (Mat 18:28), and the others were very sorry (Mat 18:31). Paul calls Epaphras “our dear fellowservant… a faithful minister of Christ” (Col 1:7). And the angel in Revelation twice refuses worship: “See thou do it not: for I am thy fellowservant… worship God” (Rev 19:10; 22:9).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines fellow-servant as one who has the same master.
webster_full: FELLOW-SERVANT, n. One who has the same master.
FELLOW, n. A companion; an associate.
2. One of the same kind; an equal.
scriptures: But the same servant went out, and found one of his fellowservants, which owed him an hundred pence: and he laid hands on him, and took him by the throat, saying, Pay me that thou owest.
So when his fellowservants saw what was done, they were very sorry, and came and told unto their lord all that was done.

And I fell at his feet to worship him. And he said unto me, See thou do it not: I am thy fellowservant, and of thy brethren that have the testimony of Jesus: worship God: for the testimony of Jesus is the spirit of prophecy.
Col 1:7
As ye also learned of Epaphras our dear fellowservant, who is for you a faithful minister of Christ;
corruption_summary: Standing among Christians is measured by office and visibility, and an angel in glory declines worship on the ground that he and John have the same Master.
corruption_paragraphs: Revelation 19:10 is one of the most levelling sentences in Scripture. John falls at the feet of a being of overwhelming glory, and the reply is: see thou do it not: I am thy fellowservant, and of thy brethren that have the testimony of Jesus: worship God. An angel places himself on the same footing as a man in exile on Patmos, because both belong to one Master. Whatever hierarchy exists in heaven, it does not licence receiving worship.

Matthew 18:28 uses the word to sharpen the parable's offence: the same servant went out, and found one of his fellowservants. Not a debtor from outside — a man in the identical position, serving the identical lord, who had just been forgiven ten thousand talents himself. The other servants' response is recorded as grief rather than anger: they were very sorry, and came and told their lord all that was done.
roots_summary: Greek sundoulos (G4889), fellow-slave; doulos (G1401), a bondservant — the status shared.
roots_lines: Greek sundoulos (G4889) — fellowservant; Matthew 18:28-33, 24:49, Colossians 1:7, 4:7, Revelation 6:11, 19:10, 22:9.
Greek doulos (G1401) — bondservant, slave; the underlying status.
Greek proskuneo (G4352) — to worship; Revelation 19:10, what the angel refused.
usage: “I am thy fellowservant… worship God” — an angel declining worship.
“Found one of his fellowservants” — identical position, identical lord.
“Our dear fellowservant” — Paul's word for Epaphras.

pos: adj. (of or like fire; rendering Hebrew saraph, Greek puroo)
etymology: From fire. Scripture's fiery things are serpents, furnaces, darts, and one trial the church is told not to find strange.
biblical_def: Fiery means of fire. Numbers records the fiery serpents and the brasen one lifted on a pole (Num 21:6–8), which Christ applies to Himself (Joh 3:14). Daniel's companions are cast into “the burning fiery furnace” and a fourth walks with them (Dan 3:20–25). Paul names “the fiery darts of the wicked” quenched by faith's shield (Eph 6:16), and Peter says, “think it not strange concerning the fiery trial which is to try you” (1Pe 4:12).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines fiery as consisting of fire; hot like fire; vehement; ardent; passionate; and unrestrained.
webster_full: FIERY, a. Consisting of fire; as the fiery gulf of Etna.
2. Hot like fire; as a fiery heat.
3. Vehement; ardent; very active; impetuous; as a fiery spirit.
4. Passionate; easily provoked; irritable.
5. Unrestrained; fierce.
scriptures: Dan 3:25
He answered and said, Lo, I see four men loose, walking in the midst of the fire, and they have no hurt; and the form of the fourth is like the Son of God.
Num 21:8
And the LORD said unto Moses, Make thee a fiery serpent, and set it upon a pole: and it shall come to pass, that every one that is bitten, when he looketh upon it, shall live.
Eph 6:16
Above all, taking the shield of faith, wherewith ye shall be able to quench all the fiery darts of the wicked.
Beloved, think it not strange concerning the fiery trial which is to try you, as though some strange thing happened unto you:
corruption_summary: Severe trial is read as evidence something has gone wrong, and Peter tells the church not to find it strange — as though some strange thing happened unto you.
corruption_paragraphs: 1 Peter 4:12 addresses the instinct directly: beloved, think it not strange concerning the fiery trial which is to try you, as though some strange thing happened unto you. The surprise is what Peter targets, not the suffering. Christians who expect exemption experience trial as a category error — something has malfunctioned — and the disorientation compounds the pain. Peter's remedy is to reset the expectation before the fire arrives.

Daniel 3:25 supplies the detail everything else rests on: lo, I see four men loose, walking in the midst of the fire, and they have no hurt; and the form of the fourth is like the Son of God. They were bound going in and loose inside. The only thing the fire consumed was the ropes, and the King who noticed was the one who had lit it.
roots_summary: Hebrew saraph (H8314), fiery, a burning one — the seraph and the fiery serpent share the root; Greek purosis (G4451), a burning; puroo (G4448), to set on fire.
roots_lines: Hebrew saraph (H8314) — fiery serpent, seraph; Numbers 21:6-8, Isaiah 6:2.
Greek purosis (G4451) — fiery trial, burning; 1 Peter 4:12, Revelation 18:9.
Greek puroo (G4448) — to set on fire; Ephesians 6:16, the fiery darts.
usage: “Four men loose, walking in the midst of the fire” — the ropes were all that burned.
“Think it not strange concerning the fiery trial” — the surprise targeted.
“Quench all the fiery darts of the wicked” — the shield raised beforehand.
